column2: Sounded legit. You check later and it was close enough.
He knows you're lying. He always knows.
Afghanistan. Village elders want a school built before they'll share intel on insurgents. What will you do?
The elders nod politely and tell you nothing.
A local warlord fighting your enemy wants machine guns. He's also known for brutality. What will you do?
He works with someone else. You sleep fine.
He crushes the insurgents. You don't ask how.
Human rights groups document what he did with your guns.
A drone feed shows a high-value target in a compound. Two children are playing in the courtyard. What will you do?
The target leaves. The kids are fine. You'll get another chance.
Target killed. So are others. You think about it every day.
Your team sees armed men approaching a partner checkpoint. They haven't fired. ROE says hostile intent is required. What will you do?
They're a local militia going home. Crisis averted.
They were insurgents. You were right.
violation of the rules of engagement
You control $100k of emergency project funds in {country}. A local contractor offers a 10% kickback. What will you do?
You're appointed to investigate an allegation that a team member assaulted a contractor. He's a legend in the unit. What will you do?
The facts are the facts. Justice done.
The IG finds out. Now you're under investigation.
Your partner commander wants to execute a captured ISIS fighter. 'He killed my brother.' What will you do?
The prisoner goes to a detention facility.
He does it anyway when you leave.
You hear the shot from the truck.
An aid worker is being held in a village in {country}. You have one window to hit it at night. What will you do?
Hostage rescued. All your men home. Bronze Star.
The hostage is moved. The window closes.
Some quiet civilians with good beards want to borrow your team for 'a thing.' No paperwork. What will you do?
They roll their eyes but send a memo.
Fascinating night. You can never talk about it.
Nobody told your colonel. He's livid.
In {country}, the ambassador wants your team to stay far from the border region. Your intel says that's where you're needed. What will you do?
The ambassador approves a limited presence.
Q Course officer phase. Your plan has a hole the instructor is about to find. What will you do?
Your best paid informant names a rival as an insurgent leader. The rival owns land your informant wants. What will you do?
The rival is just a farmer. You fire the informant.
You raided an innocent family's home.
A journalist wants to embed with your team in {country}. Public affairs approves. Your team sergeant hates it. What will you do?
Fair article. Your team looks professional.
The PAO complains to your colonel.
Your team's mortars got shipped to the wrong country. Mission is in 72 hours. What will you do?
A Ranger S4 owes you one. Mortars delivered.
Sandstorm rolls in. Your team is carrying a wounded partner. The helicopter says they can't land. What will you do?
You walk 8 km through the storm. He lives.
Storm passes. Bird lands. Close one.
He doesn't make it through the night.
You're selected for Command and General Staff College. Year of PowerPoint, golf, and essays. What will you do?
Staying on teams. Your career prospects narrow.
Your kid's birthday party is on a video call. You're in {country} and the connection keeps dropping. What will you do?
Your kid laughs at the frozen frame of your face. Good memory.
A captured fighter may know about a planned attack. {buddy} suggests 'stress techniques.' What will you do?
Rapport works. He gives you the plan.
He doesn't talk. Attack happens elsewhere.
He talks. You're never the same.
A partner nation general wants your team to train his personal guard, not the frontline troops. What will you do?
His guards are good now. The front still collapses.
As a major commanding an SF company, you have six ODAs and too many missions. What will you do?
You say no to the bad missions. Teams love you.
Teams are exhausted. Divorce rates spike.
Village Stability Operations. You live in the village with your team. Insurgents threaten the local police chief. What will you do?
The attack comes. You repel it. Village trusts you.
He's safe. The village thinks you abandoned it.
Your vehicle convoy must cross a pass known for ambushes. Higher wants you on the road today. What will you do?
killed in an ambush on a mountain pass
End of deployment. You write awards for your team. Higher says 'no Bronze Stars for support guys.' What will you do?
Every man gets what he earned.
Your commo sergeant gets a certificate.
Your rater says you're the second-best captain in the battalion. Only one can be 'Most Qualified.' What will you do?
As group commander, you must cut 15% of the budget. Options: training, language school, or dive teams. What will you do?
Teams start deploying without speaking the language. Ouch.
Congress wants answers on why soldiers died in a remote African ambush. You're called to testify. What will you do?
The families get answers. Some careers end. Not yours.
A general wants your partner force training numbers inflated for a briefing to Congress. What will you do?
He gets someone else to do it. Your next job is in a basement.
A major TV network wants to interview you about Green Beret operations. PAO is nervous. What will you do?
One quote goes viral. Wrong way.
A mother whose son died on your watch asks you directly: 'Was it worth it?' What will you do?
You tell her what he did and why. She holds your hand.
She sees through it. You see through it.
A partner country's defense minister gifts you a solid gold watch. The ethics rules are very clear. What will you do?
It goes to the government archives. You feel lighter.
Your group has lost three soldiers to suicide this year. What will you do?
Embedded psychologists in each battalion. The stigma starts to crack.
A video of brutal hazing in one of your battalions goes viral. What will you do?
It gets worse. You're relieved of command.
Washington orders a withdrawal that leaves your Syrian partners exposed. What will you do?
You write a stinging memo. You follow orders.
You're offered a cushy Pentagon job or another tour in command. What will you do?
Your star chances rise. Your soul shrinks.
You love it. Promotion odds drop.
You wake up in {country} with something long and cold moving in your sleeping bag. What will you do?
It leaves. You don't sleep again for a week.
You fly out of the bag and the team laughs for days.
It bites on the way out.
A scrappy stray dog adopts your team in {country}. Regulations say no pets. What will you do?
The dog barks at insurgents and becomes a legend.
You pay to ship it to the States. It's now living its best life.
A care package from a school in Ohio arrives with crayon drawings and 40 lbs of beef jerky. What will you do?
You hear a pop in your shoulder going for a deadlift PR in front of the team. What will you do?
Six weeks of bands and ice. Back to full strength.
It heals on its own. Lucky.
A hurricane is bearing down on Fort Bragg. Your unit is tasked to help evacuate the local area. What will you do?
You carry grandmas out of flooded houses.
A villager you helped years ago tracks you down on social media to say thanks. Her daughter is a doctor now. What will you do?
You stare at the message for a long time. This is why.
The last MRE in the box. It's Veggie Omelet. {buddy} is hungrily eyeing it. What will you do?
{buddy} eats it, gags, and thanks you. True friendship.
Pararescue Indoctrination Course. The instructors make you do underwater laps with no breaks. Your vision is going dark at the edges. What do you do?
You touch the wall and gasp. Instructor nods.
You black out. Instructors drag you up. Shallow water blackout scare.
Safe, but it's a fail. You'll have to redo it.
Efficient and calm. You make it.
Buddy breathing drill: you and {buddy} share one snorkel while instructors harass you. He's hogging the air. What do you do?
You both panic and surface. Fail.
You get air. Instructor wasn't looking.
It's week three of Indoc. Half the class is gone. You're freezing, sore and nobody would blame you for quitting. What do you do?
You stop thinking about the end and focus on the next meal.
You quit. The regret lasts years.
That Others May Live. You hold onto it.
Fins swim in choppy water. A cramp seizes your calf halfway through. What do you do?
It loosens up. You finish on time.
Safety boat picks you up. You'll retest.
Combat Diver Course in Panama City. Your rebreather is acting up during a night dive. What do you do?
Oxygen toxicity seizure. Your buddy saves you.
At military freefall school, your body position is unstable and you keep spinning. Your instructor is next to you in the air. What do you do?
You pull while unstable. Line twists. Hard landing.
He signals legs out. It works.
The paramedic phase is brutal. Pharmacology exams, clinical rotations, and you're sleeping four hours a night. How do you keep up?
You pass. Your study group becomes family.
The group is more social than studious.
You fail the cardiology exam. Retest.
During a civilian ER rotation, a gunshot victim comes in. The nurse tells you to get an IV in now. Your hands are shaking. What do you do?
You blow the vein. She does it herself.
Wrong site. The doctor takes over.
You graduate from the Pararescue Apprentice Course. An old PJ hands you the maroon beret. How do you mark the day?
You read the names of the fallen. You understand the beret now.
A long night of stories and laughter.
Your dad can't stop saying 'my son the PJ'.
You're on alert in {country}. The radio goes off: 'Pedro, Pedro, Pedro.' A helicopter is down. What's your first move?
Glad you did. You'll need everything.
The team waits on you. Not great.
Your Pave Hawk lands under fire to pick up a wounded soldier. Rounds are snapping overhead. He's 50 meters away. What do you do?
You drag him back to the bird. Wheels up.
Gunners silence the enemy. Then you go.
A soldier's leg is nearly severed by an IED. Your first tourniquet isn't stopping the bleeding. What do you do?
He bleeds out in the helicopter.
Despite everything you did, a young Marine dies in your helicopter. You can't stop thinking about it. What do you do?
He tells you about his first loss. It helps.
His mother writes back. She thanks you for being there.
Hoist training over trees. The rotor wash is spinning you on the cable. What do you do?
You slam into a tree trunk.
{buddy} wants to fill the team leader's truck with packing peanuts. It would be legendary. Are you in?
He laughs for days and swears revenge.
Night jump into the ocean with a zodiac boat. You land tangled in your canopy lines. Waves are breaking over you. What do you do?
You free yourself and reach the boat.
You swallow a lot of seawater.
A hiker is stranded on a ledge in a training area. Your team leader asks you to rappel down to him. Wind is picking up. What do you do?
Rescue successful. The hiker hugs you.
A gust slams you into the cliff.
The wind dies down. Safe rescue an hour later.
Your med bag is missing a chest seal before a mission. Supply is closed. What do you do?
An improvised chest seal works fine in the field.
There's a party in the barracks. Someone brought something a lot stronger than beer. A random drug test is likely next week. What do you do?
Three people pop on the test. You don't.
Your annual PJ fitness test includes a 25-meter underwater swim and pull-ups. You've been slacking. What do you do?
In the altitude chamber, the instructor has you remove your mask to see hypoxia symptoms. You feel giddy. What do you do?
Searching for a downed pilot's beacon in a forest. Your signal is weak and bouncing. What do you do?
You fall out of the tree.
Too slow. Another team finds him first.
After a disaster rescue, you find a scared dog in the rubble. Your team leader says no animals on the aircraft. What do you do?
A family adopts it. You see a photo later.
The crew adopts it as a mascot.
A soldier pulled from an icy river is barely breathing. He's cold to the touch. What do you do?
He stabilizes. 'Not dead until warm and dead.'
His heart goes into a bad rhythm.
Driving home, you come across a bad car crash. No ambulance yet. You have your personal med kit. What do you do?
You stabilize the driver. The news calls you a hero.
The driver doesn't make it. You did everything right.
You roll your ankle during a training jump. A long-awaited course starts next week. What do you do?
You miss the course but heal properly.
It breaks on the first day.
During a trauma lane exercise, two moulaged patients scream for help at once. One is bleeding, one isn't breathing. Who first?
Too slow on the second patient.
During a training swim, {buddy} gets stung by a jellyfish and starts panicking. What do you do?
He's fine. Owes you a beer.
He kicks you in the face.
At SERE school, you're hungry for days. You find a lizard. Do you eat it?
The team decides to give you a nickname after you fell out of the helicopter cabin in training. They pick 'Gravity'. How do you react?
An F-16 pilot ejected over hostile territory in {country}. His beacon is active but enemy trucks are moving toward him. What's the plan?
You reach him first. He cries when he sees you.
The trucks arrive at the same time.
A-10s clear the area. Clean pickup.
The enemy reaches him first. He's captured.
Enemy chases the decoy. You get the pilot.
They split up. You fight your way in.
A rocket hits a base dining hall. 20 wounded, three PJs. You're the senior medic on scene. How do you triage?
Some patients deteriorate faster than expected.
Two patients: a US soldier with minor wounds and an enemy fighter who's critical. Your team leader says treat the American. What do you do?
The fighter dies. You think about it for years.
A helicopter crashed at 11,000 feet in {country}. The air is thin and snow is coming. Survivors may be inside. What do you do?
You find two survivors. Both make it.
Safer, but nobody survives the night.
A daring hoist through a cloud gap. Survivors out.
The bird loses power at altitude.
A cargo ship crewman went overboard 600 miles out. You'll jump from an HC-130 at night into 15-foot seas. Do you lead the jump?
You find him alive after four hours.
Hard landing in the swells. You still find him.
You're on standby for a crewed capsule splashdown. If something goes wrong, PJs jump in. The capsule hits rough water. What do you do?
You stabilize the capsule. Astronauts safe.
Swells slam you into the capsule.
Your patient's blood type tag says O-negative but the bracelet says A-positive. You have only O-negative blood. What do you do?
You keep seeing the faces of the patients you couldn't save. You haven't slept properly in weeks. What do you do?
It's not weakness. It saved you.
He gets it. You start to heal.
Hurricane floods. Families stranded on rooftops. Your Pave Hawk has fuel for four more hoists. Five roofs. Who do you leave?
Another crew reaches the last roof. Everyone lives.
You save everyone and land on fumes.
Emergency landing in a parking lot. Not great.
A patient has a tension pneumothorax. The needle decompression didn't hold. The bumpy ride makes it worse. What do you do?
Air rushes out. He breathes again.
You're promoted to team leader. A young PJ keeps freezing during live missions. What do you do?
He becomes one of your best PJs.
Safer for the team. He's crushed.
The hoist cable jams with you and a patient 40 feet below the helicopter. The pilot can't hold hover much longer. What do you do?
They lower you to the ground. Plan B works.
The ground is rougher than expected.
A downed pilot is hiding in a ravine. Enemies are searching nearby. His radio is breaking up. What do you tell him?
He stays still. You find him first.
A team member fell 30 feet into a cave. He's conscious but has a spinal injury. Extraction will take hours. What do you do?
An earthquake in {country}. A child is trapped under concrete and the building is unstable. Engineers say no. What do you do?
You pull her out minutes before the building collapses.
Nobody goes in. You hear her crying for hours.
A helicopter ditched in the ocean. The crew is trapped inside at 30 feet. Visibility is near zero. What do you do?
You pull two crew members out alive.
Divers arrive. It's a recovery now.
After 16 years, your body is breaking down. Your family wants you to retire at 20. Your team wants you for one more deployment. What do you do?
Your experience saves lives. Your knees hate you.
You shield him. He's fine. You're bruised.
You're fine. The patient is worse.
The pilot says the weather is too bad to fly. A soldier will die without evacuation. What do you do?
The pilot agrees. You make it.
He refuses. You're angry for weeks.
You keep the soldier alive all night. He makes it.
A soldier has burns on 60% of his body. He's screaming. You have limited morphine. What do you do?
He calms. You focus on fluids.
His airway was swelling. You saved him.
A news crew filmed your team hoisting a stranded hiker off a cliff. They want an on-camera interview with the 'hero'. What do you say?
You name the pilots and the flight engineer. Classy.
Quiet professional. The clip goes viral anyway.
The team prints your quote and tapes it to your locker.
You're in open ocean holding a survivor, waiting 20 minutes for the helicopter. A large shark starts circling. What do you do?
It loses interest. Worst 20 minutes of your life.
It bumps, then bites your fin and leg.
Face it and jab its nose
It veers off and doesn't come back.
{buddy} wants you both to get the PJ guardian angel tattoo after this deployment. Your spouse hates tattoos. Do you get it?
Matching angels. Your spouse rolls their eyes and secretly likes it.
He gets it alone and shows it off for a month.
A private medical contractor offers you triple your pay to work as an overseas medic. You're two years from a pension. What do you do?
The money is great. You miss the team within a month.
Two more years. The team is glad you stayed.
Your spouse says your kids barely know you. You were away 200 days last year between deployments and schools. What do you do?
Your kids start running to the door when you get home.
Your career soars. The house feels colder.
Two weeks, no phone. It helps a lot.
You get recalled on day three.
A soldier collapses on a 120-degree patrol in {country}. He's confused and hot to the touch. Ice is limited. What do you do?
His temperature drops fast. He walks out of the hospital.
He seizes before you can cool him.
You're a freefall instructor. Your student's main chute streamers below you and he's not cutting away. What do you do?
You reach him and signal cutaway. Reserve opens. He lives.
You collide with him. Both reserves open, both of you hurt.
He hears you and cuts away. Reserve opens.
His automatic device fires late. He survives, badly hurt.
A mass casualty exercise has 100 screaming role players. Your team is overwhelmed and evaluators are watching. What do you do?
Evaluators note it. Knowing your limits is the point.
Your Pave Hawk clips a power line during a night approach. Alarms scream and the aircraft lurches. What do you do?
The pilots wrestle it down. Hard landing. Everyone lives.
You strap him down just in time. He's unhurt.
A PJ you served with for 10 years was killed on a rescue. His widow asks you to speak at the funeral. What do you say?
The church laughs and cries at the same time. She hugs you.
Dignified. You can't trust your voice for more.
You're asked to inventory a fallen teammate's belongings before they're sent home. You find things his wife shouldn't see. What do you do?
His family remembers him the way he'd want.
By the book. It causes his family pain.
A snowmobiler fell through a frozen lake near your base in Alaska. Local rescuers are 40 minutes out. Your team is 5 minutes away. What do you do?
You crawl across the ice and pull him out alive.
The ice breaks under you too. Your team hauls you both out.
He grabs it with frozen hands. Out.
His hands can't grip. Too cold.
A sailor on a fishing ship 800 miles at sea has a burst appendix. You'd parachute in from an HC-130 and treat him for two days. Do you jump?
You land next to the ship and keep him alive until port.
Rough water landing. He still lives, thanks to your partner.
They nail it. Good to see.
Night before your first combat rescue alert shift. {buddy} can't sleep and keeps asking 'what if'. What do you do?
You both admit you're scared. You both sleep.
At a crowded beach on leave, a lifeguard is struggling with an unconscious swimmer. You're a trained paramedic. What do you do?
He coughs up water and breathes. The crowd claps.
Paramedics take over. You did everything you could.
You watch from the sand. It bothers you.
An instructor in the Apprentice Course says your casualty care is sloppy and you'll get someone killed. It stings. How do you respond?
He spends an extra hour with you. You get better.
He makes you redo the lane five times.
You're at Combat Rescue Officer selection. After a 20-hour day, the board asks why you didn't just become a pilot. What do you say?
You talk about the pilots who came home because of PJs. Selected.
It sounds rehearsed. Not selected this year.
The old CRO on the board laughs out loud. Selected.
The pilot on the board does not laugh.
Admit you failed the eye exam
They wonder if this is your second choice.
You must plan a rescue for a downed crew 200 miles inside {country}. You have one HC-130 for fuel and two Pave Hawks. What's the plan?
In, refuel, pick up, out. The crew is home by breakfast.
The enemy guessed the obvious route. You divert.
Air defenses chase ghosts while you grab the crew.
Timing collapses. The tanker is in the wrong place.
Weather is marginal and the downed pilot's radio battery is dying. {co} asks you for a go or no-go recommendation right now. What do you say?
You thread the weather and find him with minutes of battery left.
Icing forces an abort halfway there.
The weather clears and he's still hiding. Clean pickup.
By dawn, his radio is silent.
The 'pilot' on the radio isn't using his authentication words correctly. It could be stress, or it could be a trap. What do you do?
It was just a rattled pilot. You bring him home.
Muzzle flashes erupt as you land. It was a trap.
He knows his dog's name. Verified. Clean pickup.
The delay lets a patrol close in. He's captured.
Drone shows him alone. Safe rescue.
The drone is late. Hours lost.
One slot left on a dangerous rescue. A veteran PJ with two kids, or an eager new guy who's never been tested. Who do you pick?
Calm hands, clean mission. Experience matters.
He's brilliant under pressure. A star is born.
He hesitates at a key moment. Everyone's fine, barely.
You're offered a Pentagon staff job. Great for your career, but you'd leave your squadron right before a deployment. What do you do?
You learn the budget game. Your old team sends memes about your desk.
Your PJs notice. You'll go next cycle.
During your mission brief, a junior PJ raises his hand and points out a real flaw in your fuel plan. Everyone is watching you. What do you do?
The team trusts you more. And you don't run out of gas.
The Pave Hawk lands with fuel warnings blaring. He was right.
You're running a joint rescue cell with allied forces. Their commander wants to lead the next recovery. What do you do?
They do great. The alliance is stronger.
Language confusion slows the launch by an hour.
They feel sidelined and stop sharing intel.
They handle security, you handle medicine. Perfect.
Two bosses, one radio net. Messy.
Your promotion board meets next month. Your record is good, not great. Your mentor says one more deployment would help. What do you do?
A pilot your team rescued wants to thank you on a national morning show. Public affairs is thrilled. What do you do?
You name every PJ on air. Recruiting numbers spike.
Your team gets the spotlight they earned.
Public affairs is disappointed. Quiet professionals, though.
Your squadron's training budget gets slashed. You can fund combat dive or military freefall requalification, not both. What stays?
Maritime rescue stays sharp. Freefall currency lapses.
Deep-insertion stays ready. The divers grumble.
You find leftover year-end money. Both funded.
Higher tells you to stop asking.
A PJ dies during a water training exercise you planned. The safety investigation starts tomorrow. How do you handle it?
Investigators find an equipment failure. You still lose sleep.
The board sees you as defensive. Career damage.
As a CRO, you can fly on tonight's dangerous rescue or run it from the ops center with better comms. Where do you go?
Your PJs see you on the hoist. Respect earned.
A round punches through the cabin and into your leg.
You coordinate fighters, tankers and the helos perfectly.
An allied pilot is down in contested territory. Your tasking says US personnel only, but you're closest. What do you do?
Approved in eight minutes. He's rescued.
Denied. Another nation's team arrives too late.
He's rescued. His government sends a thank-you letter.
Rescue works. You're relieved for disobeying.
After a deployment with heavy losses, your squadron's morale is in the basement. Two PJs have put in separation papers. What do you do?
Barbecue, kids, and a bounce house. It helps more than you'd think.
Embedded mental health makes a real difference.
Nobody wants to be seen going.
Two more separation papers land on your desk.
Your Pave Hawk takes fire on final approach to the survivor. The pilot looks at you. You're the mission commander. What's the call?
Gunships clear the area. You go back in and get him.
The survivor is moved by the enemy before you return.
Thirty seconds on the ground. Survivor aboard. Gone.
Rounds rake the cabin. Two crew wounded, you among them.
A PJ under your command gave the wrong drug dose during a rescue. The patient survived. He comes to you, terrified. What do you do?
A no-fault review fixes a confusing drug kit layout.
The hospital flags it. Now it's a cover-up.
You're offered a two-year exchange tour with a British rescue unit. Your spouse would have to move overseas. What do you do?
You learn their mountain tactics. And how to queue properly.
Your spouse is relieved. Another officer goes.
A typhoon flattened coastal towns in an allied nation. You're leading the US rescue element. Where do you focus first?
Your teams pull 40 people from collapsed homes in two days.
Your PJs relieve exhausted local medics.
You reach villages no one else could. Hundreds helped.
Your father has days to live. A critical recovery mission launches in 48 hours and you're the only CRO qualified. What do you do?
You hold his hand at the end. Your deputy runs the mission fine.
The mission succeeds. You miss the funeral. It haunts you.
You're teaching survival skills to a group of fighter pilots. One senior pilot says it's beneath him and refuses to participate. What do you do?
You tell him about a pilot who lived because of this class. He's first in line.
He's ordered to participate. He sulks all week.
After a successful rescue, a PJ admits he skipped a required safety step to reach the patient faster. It worked. What do you do?
He learns judgment matters. Others may cut corners now, though.
He's annoyed, but the standard holds.
